issues.legal_issue: A proceeding pending under a repealed rent law ordinarily continues under that law, subject to modifications or clarifications made by the replacement law.
material_facts: The eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent control law and remained pending when the replacement rent control law came into force.
The replacement law’s corresponding eviction provision omitted the word “suitable” from the description of residential accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The pending suit was to be continued and decided under the earlier law, with any slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement law taken into account; the change at issue did not alter the result in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, read with its first proviso, pending proceedings ordinarily continue under the repealed Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, while slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement Act apply. The Court relied on Karam Singh Sobhi v. Pratap Chand and Brij Kishore v. Vishwa Mitter Kapur.

predicates.pending_eviction_proceeding_under_repeal: An eviction proceeding under an earlier rent law remained pending when that law was repealed.
predicates.replacement_law_slightly_modifies_or_cla: The replacement rent law made only a slight modification or clarification to the relevant prior rule.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding under an earlier rent law remains pending and the replacement law only slightly modifies or clarifies the prior rule, the proceeding continues under the prior rule subject to that modification or clarification.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot be evicted solely for acquiring residential accommodation when the tenancy was for both residence and professional use.
material_facts: The rent deed described the premises as being for residence, and a letter from the landlord permitted the tenant to have a professional office there along with his residence.

The tenant used rooms in the premises as his legal practice office while living there with his family; the courts below found that the premises had been let for combined residential and professional purposes.
After the tenant died, his family continued to occupy the premises, and the respondent sons also used them for legal offices.
The respondents had built a residential house, and the landlord sought eviction on the ground that they had acquired residential accommodation.
The courts below made a concurrent finding that the tenancy was for combined residential and professional purposes.
issues.conclusion: Eviction could not be ordered merely because the tenant or his successors had acquired residential accommodation, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13(1)(h) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, do not permit eviction on the ground of acquiring residential accommodation where the tenancy is for both residence and professional use: residential accommodation alone does not satisfy the professional purpose of that tenancy. The definition of “premises” in Section 2(g) of the earlier Act, unchanged in the replacement Act, accommodates combined uses. The Court applied Dr. Gopal Das Verma v. Dr. S. K. Bhardwaj, rejected a dominant-intention test, and held that the concurrent finding of combined use foreclosed the argument that professional use was merely a personal licence ending on the original tenant’s death.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding governed by rent control law.
predicates.eviction_sought_for_acquisition_of_resid: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant or the tenant’s successors had acquired residential accommodation.
predicates.tenancy_authorized_for_residence_and_pro: The premises were let or authorized for both living there and carrying on professional work there.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding rests on acquisition of residential accommodation but the tenancy was authorized for both residence and professional use, eviction is unavailable solely on that acquisition ground.
